#9808. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9807. How I Used a Stock Market Theory to Predict Cellular Network Behavior

Dr. K. Mithra is an independent researcher in Scottsdale, Arizona, working across antennas, 5G/6G wireless, and applied AI.

Dr. K. Mithra is an independent researcher in Scottsdale, Arizona, working across antennas, 5G/6G wireless, and applied AI.

Dr. K. Mithra is an independent researcher in Scottsdale, Arizona, working across antennas, 5G/6G wireless, and applied AI.

The strangest paper I have ever written started with a stock chart.

In 2016, I was working on handoff prediction for cellular networks, the problem of anticipating when a moving phone should jump from one base station to the next. Get it right and the call continues seamlessly. Get it wrong and the call drops, the video buffers, the user curses the carrier. The standard tools were signal-strength thresholds and mobility models, and they all shared a weakness: they reacted to the network instead of anticipating it.

Around the same time, I found myself reading about Elliott wave theory. If you have never encountered it, here is the sixty-second version. In the 1930s, an accountant named Ralph Nelson Elliott noticed that stock market prices do not move randomly. They move in repetitive wave patterns, five waves forward, three waves back, driven by the collective psychology of crowds swinging between optimism and pessimism. The patterns repeat at every timescale, from minutes to decades. Traders have argued about its predictive power ever since, but the core observation is hard to dismiss: human crowds generate structure, and that structure rhymes.

And then the thought that would not leave me alone: crowds also move through cities in waves.

Think about it. Morning commute, lunch hour, evening rush, stadium emptying after a match. Thousands of phones crossing cell boundaries in rhythmic, quasi-periodic surges. The handoff load at a base station is not random noise. It is crowd behavior rendered in signaling traffic, and crowd behavior has patterns. If Elliott's waves could describe the mood swings of markets, why could they not describe the movement swings of a city?

I brought the idea to my colleagues, and I will be honest: the first reaction was the one you are probably having now. What does the stock market have to do with cell towers? Fair question. But strip away the finance vocabulary and Elliott wave theory is really a claim about self-similar patterns in time series generated by collective human behavior. Network signaling traffic is exactly that kind of time series. The domain changes; the mathematics of waves does not care.

We built a handoff prediction method around wave-pattern analysis of network traffic. Instead of waiting for a signal threshold to trip, the approach looks for the rhythmic structure in boundary-crossing activity and projects it forward, the way a surfer reads a swell rather than reacting to the water already under the board.

The work went through peer review and was published in 2016 as 'Experimental Study on Elliott Wave Theory for Handoff Prediction' in Fluctuation and Noise Letters — which in this field means it survived the scrutiny of reviewers who were at least as skeptical as you are.

Did it beat every conventional method on every metric? No, and I will not claim that. What it did was demonstrate something I find more valuable: a completely foreign mathematical framework, imported from finance, could say something true about wireless networks. The patterns held. The predictions worked well enough to stand alongside established approaches, and in bursty, crowd-driven scenarios, the wave structure captured dynamics that threshold methods missed entirely.

Here is the part I actually want you to take away, because it is bigger than one paper.

Engineering education trains us to go deep. Pick a lane, master its tools, publish in its journals. Depth matters enormously. But some of the best ideas I have encountered in twenty years of research came from sideways reading. Antenna designers who studied optics. Signal processing borrowed from seismology. And yes, handoff prediction borrowed from a stock-market accountant in the 1930s.

The mechanism is simple. Every field develops blind spots, assumptions so baked in that nobody questions them. Wireless engineers assumed handoffs were best predicted from radio measurements, because handoffs are radio events. That assumption was not wrong, but it was incomplete. Handoffs are also human-mobility events, and human mobility has been studied by urban planners, epidemiologists, and yes, market technicians. An outsider's toolkit sees what the insider's toolkit filters out.

I am not suggesting you abandon rigor for novelty. The Elliott wave idea only became a paper because we did the unglamorous work: formalizing the pattern extraction, testing against real traffic behavior, writing it up for reviewers who owed us nothing. Cross-disciplinary thinking without discipline is just tourism. But discipline without curiosity is a rut.

So here is my practical advice, especially for early-career engineers. Read one paper a month from a field that has nothing to do with yours. Not skimming, actually reading. Economics, biology, music theory, whatever pulls you. Most of it will not connect to your work. But every few years, something will click, and you will see your own problem through a lens nobody in your field is using. That is where the interesting papers live.

My path since has wound through antenna arrays, 5G channel modeling, medical imaging AI, and quantum-inspired cybersecurity. On the surface, a scattered resume. Underneath, one method: find the structure nobody else is looking at, and borrow the mathematics to describe it. It started with a stock chart and a cell tower. I have been following that instinct ever since.

Dr. K. Mithra is an independent researcher in Scottsdale, Arizona, working across antennas, 5G/6G wireless, and applied AI.

#9805. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9804. How We Stabilized a Bazel CI Runner by Fixing Resource Limits and Container Cleanup

It all started as a routing investigation.

The monorepo (Go, nodejs, C++ with shared proto files) pipeline had been running slowly for some time, and then it started to fail. Bazel builds were being OOM-killed during working hours, the retries lengthened the queue, the longer queue reduced the frequency of pushes, and the CI issues quietly escalated into engineering problems. Upon finally logging into the runner host, I found that the machine, with 6 cores and 12 threads, had a load average of 32.7. Swap space was being used. There was nothing wrong with the box in the conventional sense. It was working exactly as instructed, but the instructions themselves were bizarre.

The cause was a comment in the .bazelrc file describing a different machine. The CI configuration block briefly stated that the runner could run a maximum of two Bazel containers simultaneously, and therefore each build could consume five CPU threads and 24 GiB of memory. The calculation was correct for the target runner at the time it was written. However, the two CI tags used in the monorepo had been resolving to a different runner for quite some time, and that other runner was set to concurrent=10 with no per-job restrictions whatsoever. In other words, the machine with 6 cores and 62 GiB of memory was accepting 9 jobs at once, and each Bazel job among them was requesting the budget promised in the comment. In total, the containers on that host perceived themselves as having 25 CPUs and 120 GiB of memory. There were no cgroup limits that dictated anything else. The only restriction in the whole system was Bazel's own local_resources setting, but this setting is an estimate for the Bazel scheduler, not a hard limit.

This fix was intentionally boring and required three days of readjustment to get it working correctly. First, a hard cgroup limit was imposed on the runner, allowing three jobs with four CPUs and 14 GiB of capacity each to run simultaneously. Next, we ran four jobs using four CPUs and 12 GiB. After that, we ran five jobs using three CPUs and 11 GiB, at which point the processing stabilized. Then, with each step, .bazelrc gradually decreased from 5 CPUs and 24 GiB per build to the following:

Two of the rules within that block took me an egregious amount of time to understand. The value of local_resources must be strictly below the upper limit of cgroup. This is because if there is a margin, resource-intensive processes will be queued instead of being OOM-killed. Furthermore, the memory value should be determined based on the actually measured 6.68 GiB resident memory set, not on the 11.37 GiB working set. This is because the difference between these two values represents the reclaimable page cache that the kernel frees when needed.

There was another surprise on the CPU side. The first version of the caps used a hard CFS quota, so the box quickly went into half-idle mode. Measurements revealed that host utilization was only 50%, and the one job actually running was throttled in 93% of its CFS periods. Hard quotas serve to protect neighbors that don't yet exist, but this is achieved by tightening the limits on currently running jobs. Therefore, while the CPU limit was no longer strictly defined and a fair allocation method was adopted, the memory limit was strictly maintained. This is because memory is the resource that actually kills.

Additionally, some jobs were moved. The Starlark linter and code review helper were occupying build slots on the loaded runner, but since linters shouldn't occupy build slots, both were moved to a lighter runner. The only remaining process was the computation of the affected targets, because this process required the warm repository cache present on that machine.

While investigating the host, I discovered a second leak, older and less noticeable than the first. Our integration tests launch helper containers using the raw Docker SDK, and the CI job mounts the host's Docker socket. This means these containers are siblings of the job on the host and outlive the job. These cleanup processes are performed within a finally block, which is not executed if the job is terminated. And, since the previous pipeline is automatically canceled each time a push is made, the job is terminated periodically. The Reaper shipped by Testcontainers only owns containers that Testcontainers itself launched. The host's garbage collector only removes containers with the Testcontainers label. These helper containers did not have any labels. Its natural lifespan was 300 seconds. The specimens I found on the runner were 4 months, 8 weeks, and 3 days old.

To solve that problem, we needed to modify one line for each calling site, for a total of five lines of (vibe)code.

The monorepo behind all of this has 816 BUILD files, 151 of which define container images, so the runner isn't a toy and the load is real. However, this story isn't unique to Bazel or our stack.

The lessons I learned from this are that CI hosts follow cgroups, not comments, and all capacity promises must originate from the hosting machine, be verified against the machine's specifications, and reaffirmed when jobs begin to be run elsewhere. And, in parallel with that, every process that CI starts on a shared host needs to be labeled so that the garbage collector can read it, because finally blocks are also promises, and jobs that are terminated do not keep those promises.

#9803. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9802. Flaschendrehen Multi-Device in Flutter: Warum deterministische Physik unsere 15-Handy-Sync rettete

Wir sind das unabhängige Entwickler-Team hinter Wobbly Bottle.

In Part 1 haben wir das Konzept vorgestellt: Bei WG-Partys und Feiern hängen oft 10 Leute über einem einzigen 6-Zoll-Display. Mit Wobbly Bottle treten bis zu 15 Personen über einen 6-stelligen PIN-Code einem Raum bei – und die Flasche dreht sich synchron auf jedem einzelnen Handy.

Ein Leser auf Dev.to hat uns nach der Server-Autorität und Reconnect-Logik gefragt. Hier ist die detaillierte Architektur:

Unser erster Impuls: Wenn sich der Flaschenwinkel 60 Mal pro Sekunde ändert, senden wir den Winkel einfach per WebSocket an alle 14 anderen Handys.

Statt Bildpunkte zu übertragen, sendet der Host beim Drehen eine einzige kompakte Nachricht:

Jedes verbundene Gerät führt die identische physikalische Dämpfung in einem 60 FPS CustomPainter lokal aus:

Da alle Handys mit demselben Startimpuls und derselben Reibungsformel rechnen, stoppt die Flasche auf jedem Display im Raum auf das exakt selbe Grad.

Verliert ein Spieler kurz das Netz, spielen wir nicht mühsam alte Animationen nach. Der Client holt sich sofort einen State-Snapshot des Raums (wer ist dran, welche Karte liegt offen) und schaltet sich nahtlos wieder ein.

#9801. Microtask vs Macrotask in JavaScript — With Node.js vs Browser Notes

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at bitlyst.vercel.app

Node.js has phases in its event loop (simplified):

1) Timers → setTimeout / setInterval callbacks 2) Pending Callbacks 3) Poll → I/O callbacks; may block waiting for I/O 4) Check → setImmediate callbacks 5) Close Callbacks

After each phase, Node runs microtask queues in this order:

Tip: If you place the scheduling inside an I/O callback (e.g., fs.readFile), setImmediate is more likely to run before setTimeout.

Use process.nextTick sparingly (it’s too eager), and prefer Promise microtasks for normal “run right after” semantics.

This diagram shows how a microtask (Promise) runs before a macrotask (setTimeout) after the script finishes.

That’s it — now you can reason about microtasks/macrotasks across both environments with confidence.

#9800. 3 Personality Traits Associated With Infidelity

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

People who are low on conscientiousness are more likely to cheat on their partner, research finds.

People who are not conscientious are careless, badly organised and find it hard to resist temptation.

People who are more extraverted are also more likely to cheat on their partner, the researchers found.

It is probably because extraverted people have a wider social circle and so more opportunities to cheat.

Also, extraverts are impulsive, sensation-seekers who can easily succumb to their desires.

The conclusions come from a survey of 208 people, who were asked about their relationships and whether they had cheated.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner, the authors write:

“Early studies reported that by the age of 40, 50% of all married men and more than 25% of all married women have engaged in extramarital sexual behavior.

Three decades later, an estimated 50% of men continued to engage in sexual and/or emotional extramarital relations while 40% of women engaged in similar relationships.”

The results of the study revealed that cheaters tend to be low in conscientiousness, extraverted and open to experience.

Extraverts tend to seek out stimulation, the authors write:

“Extroverts may be inclined to cheat to obtain stimulation and prevent boredom.

Extroversion may also facilitate less investment in the relationship when those with this trait seek out others for stimulation, thereby decreasing commitment and resulting in cheating behaviours.”

The third personality trait associated with infidelity is openness to experience.

Openness to experience is linked to intellect and creativity.

“…cheaters may perceive themselves as having stronger intellect and stronger creativity compared to that of their partners, leading them to seek out partners that may be a better, that is, similar, match.”

The study was published in the journal Current Psychology (Orzeck & Lung, 2005).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. #9798. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. #9796. The state of MCP auth, November 2026: I scanned 25 public servers

MCP (Model Context Protocol) has an auth story on paper: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, dynamic client registration, resource indicators per RFC 8707. In practice I kept running into servers that were missing most of it. So I spent a week building patchbay audit, a free CLI that pokes an MCP server and reports what it finds. Then I pointed it at 25 public endpoints.

25 servers scanned on 2026-11-02. All publicly listed in community directories or vendor docs. URL list in the repo.

Three servers initially triggered critical findings. One (Chainflip's broker MCP) came back within hours documenting their public-by-design broker pattern: tools are intentionally no-auth because the actual value transfer is signed on-chain by the user. Downgraded to the same bucket I use for DeepWiki. Two embargoed findings remain under a 90-day embargo.

Public-by-design servers like DeepWiki and Chainflip are now flagged as info, public read-only or user-signed pattern rather than critical. That distinction matters more than it sounds: the first version of my tool called DeepWiki "critical no auth required", which would have made the whole write-up indefensible on day one.

patchbay audit runs 13 checks grouped roughly like this:

Auth presence (AUTH-001, AUTH-002). Does the server accept tools/list without credentials? If yes, do any tool names look mutating (create / delete / send / execute / start-...)? Critical only when both are true.

OAuth metadata completeness (AUTH-003 / 004 / 005). If the server serves /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, we read it and check for PKCE S256 advertisement, resource indicators, and a dynamic client registration endpoint.

Scopes (SCOPE-001, SCOPE-002). If the server advertises OAuth, do its tools declare per-tool scopes? Do write and read tools share a scope (so revoking write access also revokes reads)?

Secrets and transport (SECRET-001, SECRET-002, TRANSPORT-001, TRANSPORT-002, REDIRECT-001). Hardcoded sk-... / ghp_... / AKIA... in source files (skipping test fixtures). Remote-mode checks plain HTTP, spoofed Origin, loopback redirect-uri handling.

Honest probe failures (PROBE-001). If the probe can't learn anything (auth-walled, unknown transport, no response), we say so explicitly instead of returning "0 findings, all clean". That silent-false-negative trap is real when scanning diverse servers.

--ci makes it exit non-zero on critical / high so your GitHub Action fails the build. A drop-in GitHub Action posts the markdown findings as a PR comment and uploads SARIF to GitHub Code Scanning.

What I think is actually going on The MCP 2025-03-26 Streamable HTTP spec is new enough that most server implementations are catching up to it. Vendors that already have working OAuth (Linear, Notion, Supabase) tend to require auth but not necessarily serve the MCP-specific discovery documents.

The servers to worry about are the public ones with mutating tools and no documented reason for being public. Startups and solo projects shipping MCP endpoints that look like read-only wiki queries but include create_... or update_... tools in the list.

If you’re building an MCP server right now, the fastest wins are:

Serve /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource so clients can discover your auth server Advertise code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"] and resource_indicators_supported: true in your authorization server metadata Give each tool its own scope and reject calls whose token lacks it Try it npx -y @patchbay-nebius/agent audit Repo (MIT): GodSmasher/patchbay. No tracking, no backend, no account. Just a CLI.

False-positive reports are the most useful feedback right now. The severity recalibration between first and second version came entirely from running the tool on known-good servers.

Originally published at patchbay-mcp.dev/blog.

#9794. 2 Supplements That Significantly Reduce Heart Disease And Cancer Risk

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

Omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil can significantly reduce heart attacks and vitamin D supplementation can significantly lower the number of deaths caused by different types of cancer.

Researchers studied 26,000 American adults in the VITAL clinical trial for five years to see if fish oil or vitamin D would definitely ward off cardiovascular disease or cancer.

The outcomes were reassuring: marine omega-3 fatty acid intake was linked to a significant drop in heart attacks.

One-and-half servings per week of dietary fish intake showed the maximum heart health benefits, but higher dietary fish intake didn’t help more.

The greatest decrease in heart attacks was seen in African-Americans.

The benefit of 1 gram of omega-3 fish oil supplementation showed a small decrease in major cardiovascular events like stroke and death from cardiovascular disease.

Vitamin D3 or cholecalciferol intake at a dose of 2000 IU per day showed a significant decrease of death from cancer for those who took it for at least two years.

However, supplementation with vitamin D3 capsules didn’t significantly lower incidence of any type of cancer or cardiovascular disease.

Dr. JoAnn Manson, the study’s first author, said:

“The pattern of findings suggests a complex balance of benefits and risks for each intervention and points to the need for additional research to determine which individuals may be most likely to derive a net benefit from these supplements.”

Dr. Stephanie Faubion, NAMS medical director, said:

“With heart disease and cancer representing the most significant health threats to women, it is imperative that we continue to study the viability of options that prevent these diseases and help women survive them.”

The 1 gram omega-3 fish oil supplementation used in the VITAL clinical trial was Omacor, a prescription medicine for adults.

The capsule contains 840 milligrams marine omega-3 fatty acids, of which 465 mg is eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and 375 mg is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

The study was presented at the North American Menopause Society (NAMS) Annual Meeting in Chicago (Manson et al., 2019).

#9793. South Korea Wants Stablecoins Written Into Its Forex Law Within The Year

The Bank of Korea plans to prepare the bill jointly with the government before the year ends. Unhosted wallets and mixers are already on its radar.

South Korea is moving on two tracks at once.

The first is fast and narrow. The government and the Bank of Korea plan to revise the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act this year, so that stablecoins are regulated as payment instruments.

The second is slow and broad: the Digital Asset Basic Act, a comprehensive framework that the government is still developing. The forex amendment is how the central bank intends to act before that larger law arrives.

The Bank of Korea said it is coordinating with the government on measures to regulate cross-border transactions in digital assets.

Note the vehicle. The change runs through the forex law, ahead of the dedicated digital asset law still in development.

The plan answers last year's National Assembly audit.

During that audit, lawmakers asked the Bank of Korea to bring local payment infrastructure up to global standards. Two requests are on the record:

The Bank of Korea also said it would focus on building an international cooperation framework to combat illegal digital asset transactions.

Its reasoning is worth reading closely. In the central bank's view, these transactions enable cross-border transfers outside traditional financial institutions. It added that tools like mixers and unhosted wallets increase anonymity, which makes illicit activities easier to carry out.

This is the central bank's stated view, not yet a rule. But it shows which tools the institution drafting the forex amendment is watching.

For anyone holding their own keys, that is the part of this story to follow as the bill takes shape.

The Digital Asset Basic Act seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for crypto, including:

On Thursday, at a hearing, Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission, said discussions on the bill were nearing completion. He said the government will work to introduce it as soon as possible.

Until then, there is a gap. The Bank of Korea said it will continue consulting with relevant ministries to minimize regulatory arbitrage that could arise from temporary legislative gaps while the Digital Asset Basic Act takes shape.

South Korea is not waiting for its comprehensive law to define stablecoins. It is reaching for the statute it already has, the forex law, and framing stablecoins as a payment and cross-border issue first.

The pattern is clear in the central bank's own words. Cross-border flows outside traditional institutions come first, and mixers and unhosted wallets are named in the same breath as illicit activity.

The Digital Asset Basic Act will set the broad rules. The forex amendment shows where the pressure is now.

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9790. MVVM, Micro‑Frontends, and Domain‑Driven Frontend — A Practical Guide

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at bitlyst.vercel.app

This post gives you crisp mental models and copy‑pasteable patterns for three frequently‑confused topics:

TL;DR: Use MVVM to structure components, DDD to structure the system/domain, and micro‑frontends only when org/scale complexity requires independent deploys.

Model = domain data (entities/value objects). View = React UI. ViewModel = state + behaviors the View needs (pure, testable, no DOM).

Tip: A custom hook is a great ViewModel. For shared state, use a store (Zustand/Jotai) and export selectors as VM surface.

Goal: mirror business domains and bounded contexts so features don’t leak across layers.

Outcome: Separation between domain and delivery (React/UI); safer refactors, clearer ownership.

Split a large UI into independently built & deployed parts. Useful for many teams, different release cycles, or poly‑stacks.

Use MFEs when organizational complexity dominates. If one team, one repo, don’t start here.

#9788. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9787. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9786. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9784. Appsmith title matches need a self-hosted security baseline

Appsmith is a low-code application builder that can connect to databases and APIs, execute server-side queries, and expose internal tools to selected users. A self-hosted Appsmith instance is often deployed on a custom domain, which makes public inventory and ownership review especially important.

A count-only ZoomEye query on 2026-11-03 at 18:44:27 UTC found 8,380 matches for title="Appsmith" with sub_type=all, page 1, and a page size of 1. The app="Appsmith" query returned 7,833 at 18:44:29 UTC. The title view is larger, so the two sets should be sampled separately.

Appsmith's authentication documentation lists form login, OAuth, OpenID Connect, and SAML options. The self-hosting best-practices page recommends federated authentication where possible, email verification if form login remains enabled, and disabling open signups. Those recommendations describe a target baseline. They do not prove that a matched deployment follows it.

The instance may hold credentials for databases, Git repositories, and external APIs. Appsmith's security documentation describes server-side credential handling and encrypted storage for sensitive values, but an application that is reachable from the internet still needs strong account and workspace controls. A public app with a privileged query can expose data whether or not the credentials are visible in the browser.

Title matches can include documentation, hosted services, and custom front ends. Validate the page before adding it to the asset inventory. The exact ZoomEye result gives a timestamped set of candidates, while the vendor documentation gives the controls to assess once an owner is identified.

The Appsmith server appends credentials when it executes a query. That design keeps secrets out of the browser, but it also means the application must decide which user may trigger which query. A role that can edit an app may be able to change the query or attach a different data source. A role that can only view an app may still cause a privileged query to run.

Review the data-source ownership, query bindings, and app-level permissions together. Test a read-only user against a query that should be restricted. Check whether the response includes raw rows, export links, or debug details. Review any Git-backed application history for credentials or test endpoints that were committed during development.

The self-hosted baseline should include a deployment inventory, a supported version, a certificate, and an owner. A public Appsmith title with no owner is a candidate for retirement or isolation. A title with an owner but no tested query boundary is still an open security question. The count and the vendor controls point to different parts of the same review.

#9782. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9781. How I Give Every Story Its Own Cover Without a Designer

Every post on my platform has its own cover thumbnail. Every single one — more than 130 of them. I have no designer, no budget, and no laptop. Here is the system that makes it work.

First, the rule that matters most: the title on the cover is always in the story's own language. An Urdu story gets an Urdu-script title on its cover. An English story gets an English title. That sounds obvious, and it is the rule I broke most often before I made it a rule. A cover in the wrong script tells the reader, before a single word is read, that this story was not made for them. My readers notice. I notice when they notice.

Second, one image per story, and the image has to depict that story — not a generic pretty picture. A story about a clockmaker's library gets a clock, a library, a door slightly open. A story about a lost-and-found station gets the station. This is the slow part, and it is the part worth being slow about. A cover that could belong to any story belongs to no story.

Third, the pipeline is boring on purpose. New story goes up, cover gets generated the same day, same size, same title placement, same brand colours. Boring is the point: when the process is the same every time, the only decision left is the creative one — what does this story look like? I do the creative decision fresh each time and let the routine carry everything else.

The result surprised me. Readers started recognising stories by their covers before they read the titles. In the serials list, the covers do half the work of the episode titles — a returning reader spots the colour and the image and knows exactly which story they are coming back to. That was never the plan. The plan was just to stop publishing naked text. The covers turned into the platform's memory.

If you are building anything with more content than time, my advice is this: make the cover part of publishing, not an extra step after publishing. The day a story ships without a cover is the day your system has a hole in it, and holes grow. One image, one title in the right script, every time. It is the cheapest trust you can buy — and on a zero budget, it is free.

The covers live on every page of NazmHub (https://nazmhub.pages.dev), and the serials — where the cover system earns its keep daily — are at NazmHub /series (https://nazmhub.pages.dev/series). One hundred and thirty-two small promises, kept.

#9780. Your JSON is valid and your invoice is wrong

Imagine a perfectly reasonable backend refactor.

client.name becomes customer.legalName. The new shape is clearer. The JSON parses. The application tests are green.

Beautiful margins. Correct logo. No customer.

The document has successfully generated an invoice addressed to absolutely nobody.

This is an illustrative failure in a loosely checked integration, but the underlying problem is useful to think about: valid JSON tells you surprisingly little about whether a document is correct.

I'm building Bitavu, a visual template editor with a JSON-to-PDF API. The boundary between incoming data and a saved document template is one of the places where a visible error can be much more useful than a successful download.

Here is the data the template originally expected:

Both are valid JSON. Both contain the same company name.

But a template bound to client.name does not automatically understand that customer.legalName is its replacement.

If the integration quietly converts a missing value into an empty string, the PDF may still render. The mistake has simply moved from an error response into a document someone will send.

The refactor is reasonable. The unchanged binding is the problem.

Three different checks are involved here:

Structure: does it contain the paths and types the template requires?

Meaning: are those values the right ones for this document?

Some fields really are optional. An absent delivery note might reasonably leave no visible text.

A missing billing recipient deserves a different decision.

If the document requires a customer name, make that requirement explicit before rendering. Even a small guard is better than quietly substituting a blank:

This checks one field. A real document contract needs to cover its other required fields, types, arrays, and allowed values too.

Notice what happens with the refactored payload: the guard fails.

That is useful. You now have a specific integration change to review before an invoice leaves the system.

An empty string would have been quieter. The customer would have discovered the problem for you.

Now suppose the input contains both of these:

Both names are present. Both are strings. Both look like sensible things to put on a business document.

Only one belongs in this invoice's Bill to field.

This is why a mapping can be technically valid and still be wrong.

A structural validator can check that a string exists at a declared path. It cannot infer which business entity you intended to bill just because two field names look related.

When you review a mapping, ask a more useful question than "does the preview have text now?"

Ask: "Is this the person or company the document is supposed to name?"

The wrong name often looks more finished than a blank one. That does not make it a better result.

For the first example, a deliberate mapping might be:

That is a small transformation with a specific meaning: this upstream legal name supplies this template's client name.

Review it against the document's purpose. If an AI tool proposes the mapping, the same review still applies. A plausible field match is a proposal, not evidence that the two fields mean the same thing.

Before adopting it, use a few synthetic examples:

The second case is especially helpful. If every name in your fixture is "Test Company," the wrong mapping can look perfectly correct.

Give the warehouse a different name. Let your test data disagree with itself in the ways real data does.

In Bitavu, a detected schema mismatch is reported as 422 SCHEMA_DRIFT. After reviewing a transformation, you can save a mapping and reference its mappingId in render requests.

Saved mappings target a particular template revision. That gives the reviewed transformation a defined destination instead of treating it as a universal fix for every document.

Conceptual workflow illustration, not a Studio screenshot.

That mechanism helps make the mismatch explicit. It still needs a well-defined template contract and a person who understands what the fields mean.

The useful outcome is a document whose data and presentation have both been checked.

A green check beside "valid JSON" cannot do all of that work.

What is harder to catch in your documents: a missing value, or a completely believable wrong one?

Disclosure: I'm building Bitavu. All four illustrations are AI-generated conceptual scenes using synthetic examples.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.
