#9663. Holiday anxiety: causes, symptoms, and 10 ways to cope

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We often think of the holiday season as a magical time filled with joy, family gatherings, and celebrations. And it can be. However, for many people, this time of year can also usher in a wave of holiday anxiety, a type of stress associated with the many demands and expectations of the festive season.

Holiday anxiety is a specific type of stress that occurs during holiday seasons. It's different from everyday stress, because it's linked to the unique pressures and expectations that come with holiday events and traditions. Understanding holiday anxiety and recognizing its effects on our mental health can help us manage it effectively. Here are some of the ways it can manifest:

Emotional overload: The holidays can bring a range of emotions, both happy and sad. For some, reminders of lost loved ones or past experiences can lead to feelings of grief or nostalgia.

Physical symptoms: Anxiety can cause physical symptoms like headaches, fatigue, or digestive problems. These can be exacerbated by holiday indulgences and disrupted routines.

Social stress: The pressure to socialize, host events, or interact with family members you might not see regularly can be overwhelming, especially if there are a lot of late nights involved. This is especially true for those with existing social anxieties.

Routine disruption: Regular routines are often disrupted during the holidays, which can be particularly challenging for those who find comfort and stability in their daily schedules.

Acknowledge your feelings around holiday anxiety and remember that it's okay to feel stressed or overwhelmed during the holiday season. Taking proactive steps to manage your mental health can help make the holidays a more enjoyable and less stressful time.

Increased stress levels: Additional demands in the holiday season can lead to heightened stress levels, impacting mental health.

Mood fluctuations: The highs and lows can cause mood swings, bouts of sadness, irritability, and even depression.

Sleep disruption: Anxiety can disturb sleep patterns, leading to insomnia or poor-quality sleep, which, in turn, affects overall wellbeing.

Unhealthy coping mechanisms: Some people might resort to habits like overeating, excessive drinking, or withdrawing from social interactions, which can further impact their mental health.

While what triggers one person may not trigger another, there are a few ways that holiday anxiety can manifest. Identifying your unique triggers can help you prepare tools and strategies to better handle anxiety during this busy season. While the holidays can be an important time, protecting your mental health is more important.

The media and social norms often portray the holidays as a time of perfection and endless joy. This can set unrealistic expectations for the ideal holiday experience, leading to disappointment and stress when reality doesn't match these ideals.

Holidays often come with financial burdens, including the cost of gifts, travel, decorations, and hosting events. Worrying about how to afford these expenses can cause significant stress.

Holidays often feature family gatherings, which can be challenging if relationships are strained or there's a history of conflict. Navigating these dynamics, especially in larger gatherings, can bring anxiety.

The holiday season is filled with invitations to social events, expectations to meet, and tasks to complete. Trying to do everything can lead to burnout and feeling overwhelmed.

For those who’ve lost loved ones or are far from family, the holidays can intensify feelings of grief or isolation. The contrast between personal experience and the general festivity can be overwhelming.

Comparing your own holiday experience to what others seem to be doing online or social media can lead to feelings of inadequacy and dissatisfaction.

Traveling during the holidays can be chaotic and stressful because of busy airports, traffic jams, and the fear of plans being disrupted or not going as scheduled.

The change in daily routines during the holidays, such as altered eating habits, sleep schedules, and exercise, can contribute to stress and anxiety.

Managing holiday anxiety effectively involves practical strategies that focus on self-care and mindfulness. These tips can help you navigate the holiday season with less stress, more enjoyment, and better mental health.

Make a list of holiday activities and rank them in order of importance to you. Focus on the top few that bring you the most joy or are the most meaningful. This can help reduce the feeling of being overwhelmed, ensuring you spend your time and energy on what truly matters to you.

Cut back on elaborate plans. Instead, go for simpler celebrations or low-key gatherings to reduce the pressure and expectations. Smaller, intimate gatherings often bring more joy than large, stressful events.

Enjoy holiday treats but avoid overeating by listening to your body's hunger and fullness cues. Mindful eating can help you maintain physical and mental wellbeing, as overindulgence can often lead to physical discomfort and emotional guilt.

💙 Explore Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Eating Practice and learn the fundamentals of mindfulness at mealtime and how it can help your overall stress and anxiety.

Remind yourself that it’s okay for things not to be perfect, and be realistic about what you can achieve and what the holidays can offer. Having realistic expectations can significantly reduce disappointment and stress.

💙 Learn to let go of what was supposed to be and embrace what is with Jay Shetty’s guided meditation on Expectations.

Don’t pack your schedule too tightly. Instead, plan for breaks and downtime in your holiday schedule. Rest is essential for helping you to recharge, and it allows opportunities for spontaneous activities, too.

💙 When it’s time for bed, make it count by listening to Oren Jay Sofer’s guided sleep meditation, Deep Rest.

Whenever you feel stressed, take a moment to focus on your breathing. Inhale deeply for a count of four, hold for a count of four, and exhale for a count of four to help calm the mind and reduce anxiety.

💙 Use your breath to calm your mind and anxiety in three minutes with Breathe to Calm Down.

Set a budget for holiday spending and stick to it. Consider homemade gifts or shared experiences instead of expensive purchases. This can help reduce holiday anxiety caused by financial strain.

💙 Set Financial Intentions and goals this holiday season, and stick to them.

Not everything will go as planned, so be open to accepting it, and find humor and joy in the imperfect moments. Embracing imperfection can lead to a more relaxed and enjoyable holiday experience.

💙 Shift your energy from perfectionism to going with the flow with this meditation on Energy Management to help guide you toward ease.

Reduce the time you spend on social media to avoid unhealthy comparisons. Limiting social media can help maintain a more realistic perspective and reduce feelings of inadequacy.

💙 Release yourself from the Social Mania comparison by forgoing social media during the holidays.

Reach out to supportive friends, family, or a professional if you feel the holiday stress is too much to handle alone. Talking about your feelings and sharing your experiences can provide relief and remind you you’re not alone in your feelings.

The holidays can be a source of anxiety due to a combination of high expectations, financial pressures, family dynamics, and the disruption of normal routines. The holidays are often portrayed as a time of complete joy and perfect family gatherings, but when reality doesn't match up, it can lead to feelings of inadequacy or disappointment. The holidays can also be a reminder of lost loved ones or past difficulties, contributing to feelings of sadness or loneliness for many people.

The 3-3-3 rule is a simple mindfulness technique to help ground yourself during anxious moments. This exercise can help bring your focus back to the present, interrupting the cycle of anxious thoughts.

Name three things you can see around you.

Move three parts of your body, like your ankle, fingers, and shoulder.

There are plenty of actionable ways to calm holiday anxiety.

Prioritize self-care activities like mindful breathing or a relaxing bath.

Engage in regular physical activity to help relieve stress.

Keep a regular sleep schedule to ensure adequate rest.

Set realistic expectations for the holidays.

Simplify plans and focus only on what matters most to you.

Seek support from friends, family, or professionals.

It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed during Christmas. The holiday season can be a hectic time with lots of social obligations, financial pressures, and the emotional weight of personal or family expectations. It's important to recognize these feelings and take steps to manage them, like setting boundaries, asking for help when needed, and taking time for self-care.

To manage social anxiety during Thanksgiving, plan ahead for social interactions. Have some conversation topics ready to ease into interactions. Set boundaries for yourself, and step away for a moment if you feel overwhelmed. Focus on making connections with one or two people rather than trying to engage with everyone. Practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing before and during the event. And remember, it's okay to limit social gatherings to what feels manageable for you.

Yes. Anxiety can build before a trip, show up during it, or both, often from planning pressure or the work you left behind. If this is your main concern, our guide to vacation anxiety covers what to do before, during, and after your holiday.

#9660. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

#9645. 7 types of anxiety disorders (and how to deal with each one)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your heart starts racing the moment you walk into a crowded room. Even when nothing’s wrong, worry looms in the back of your mind. The thought of a specific fear, like snakes or needles, makes you feel sick. If any of that sounds familiar, anxiety might be part of the picture.

Anxiety doesn't look the same for everyone, which is sometimes why it can be so hard to name. The term "anxiety" covers several disorders, each with its own signs and triggers — though they often overlap, both in how they show up and in what helps.

Anxiety disorders affect roughly 1 in 5 U.S. adults every year. The good news is, they’re typically quite treatable. Let’s break down the seven main types of anxiety listed in the DSM-5 (the manual used for clinical diagnosis), and how to find some relief.

The seven anxiety disorders below share a general thread: they’re rooted in fear or worry that sticks around and gets in the way of daily life. They’re also the most common types, though a few related conditions are worth knowing too (covered further down).

GAD is a persistent, hard-to-control worry that spans multiple areas of your life and shows up more days than not for at least six months. Everyday stress usually has a clear cause and fades once the situation resolves. By contrast, generalized anxiety moves from topic to topic and rarely lets up, because your mind treats any uncertainty as a threat.

This disorder often comes with physical and mental symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, and disrupted sleep.

What helps: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely used for GAD. It helps you spot and shift the thought patterns that fuel your worries. A regular mindfulness practice can also ease tension by training your attention to stay in the present instead of running through what-ifs.

💙 Start with Calm’s Tools for Stress and Anxiety series.

For a more detailed overview, check out our GAD guide.

A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear that brings on physical symptoms—racing heart, tight chest, dizziness—and usually peaks within minutes. A single panic attack doesn't mean you have panic disorder — plenty of people experience one and never have another.

Panic disorder is defined by what comes after the attack, such as ongoing dread about when the next one might hit and routine changes made to avoid triggering one.

This fear response tends to feed itself in a cycle. A normal body signal, like a fast heartbeat, gets misread as danger. That triggers more fear, which leads to more physical symptoms.

What helps: CBT can help you learn to read these body signals as harmless rather than dangerous. It’s often paired with interoceptive exposure, where you deliberately bring on mild versions of those same sensations until they stop feeling threatening. During this process, slow breathing can signal safety to your nervous system.

Discover 5 mindfulness tools to calm you down during a panic attack.

Social anxiety disorder is a strong fear that you’ll be negatively perceived in social or performance situations, often severe enough that dread sets in days before the event itself.

It's much more than being shy. At its core is a belief that you'll do something embarrassing and be judged for it. That belief may lead you to avoid those situations altogether, which can bring short-term relief but reinforces the fear over time.

What helps: Exposure-based CBT has the strongest evidence. It gradually builds your comfort in the situations you've been avoiding by facing them in small, manageable steps. Self-compassion can also make a real difference. Since social anxiety tends to run on harsh self-judgment, practicing kindness toward yourself can help quiet that inner critic.

Not sure if you have social anxiety? Here are signs to look out for.

A specific phobia is a fear of one particular thing—like heights, flying, needles, dogs, or tight spaces—out of proportion to the actual danger. A fear becomes a phobia when it impacts your behavior, whether that’s rerouting a drive to avoid a bridge or skipping a checkup because of needles. Even thinking about the trigger can set off anxiety, so avoiding it becomes your default.

Phobias often start with a scary experience or a fear picked up early in life. Avoidance keeps the fear alive, since your brain never learns that the trigger is safe.

What helps: Exposure therapy is the leading treatment, shown to outperform placebo and other therapies. Pair each step with grounding and breathing techniques to make the process feel more manageable.

Explore the most common phobias and how to deal with them.

Agoraphobia is a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help if panic or embarrassing symptoms hit. This can include public transit, open spaces, crowds, lines, or long stretches away from home alone. Many people with agoraphobia avoid those places altogether.

The DSM-5 classifies it as its own diagnosis. Left untreated, this avoidance can shrink your world, sometimes making it hard to leave the house at all.

What helps: CBT with step-by-step exposure is the first-line treatment, and it helps you return to avoided places gradually. Since agoraphobia and panic often overlap, treatment usually addresses both. To build confidence, try calming techniques at home first, then in triggering places.

Learn 8 evidence-backed ways to manage agoraphobia.

Separation anxiety disorder is an excessive fear about being away from people you're close to. Once seen as a childhood condition, it’s now known to affect adults too. It can show up as real distress when a partner travels or constant worry that something bad will happen to a loved one.

Underneath it is a fear of loss: of the person or of your own ability to cope without them. You may find yourself seeking reassurance or checking in repeatedly, but these responses tend to feed the anxiety rather than calm it.

What helps: CBT can help you reduce your need for reassurance and build comfort with time apart. Mindfulness encourages you to pause when an anxious thought arises and let the worry pass. For severe cases, a doctor may suggest therapy alongside medication.

💙 Practice riding out anxious thoughts with Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety course.

Selective mutism is an inability to speak in certain social settings where talking is expected, like school or work. It's rare, affecting under 2% of people, and it usually shows up in childhood, though it can last into later years.

This isn't stubbornness or a speech problem — it's fear. You may want to speak, but hold back because of it in those environments.

What helps: Behavioral therapy that slowly builds up speaking in those settings, often involving family or school staff, is the main approach. Early intervention tends to lead to better outcomes, so it’s worth seeking professional guidance as soon as symptoms appear.

While the disorders above are what most people mean by "anxiety," a few related conditions are helpful to understand for the full picture.

Two more fall under the DSM-5's anxiety chapter:

Substance or medication-induced anxiety disorder: This anxiety is caused directly by a substance, whether that’s too much caffeine, a prescription drug, or withdrawal from alcohol. It can be overlooked, which is why a doctor will often ask what you're taking before making a diagnosis.

Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: A physical illness—such as an overactive thyroid or a heart or lung problem—can cause anxiety. A checkup can rule out this possibility early on, and treating the underlying illness often eases the anxiety too.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) get grouped with anxiety disorders a lot, as they also involve overwhelming fear and distress. But the DSM-5 classifies them separately: OCD centers on unwanted thoughts and behaviors, while PTSD comes after a traumatic event.

If either sounds closer to what you're dealing with, our OCD guide or our complex PTSD guide is a good place to start.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder differ mainly in how the worry builds and shows up. GAD involves a slow-burning worry about many areas of life that rarely fades. Panic disorder centers on sudden, intense attacks and the fear of having another one. It’s possible to have both, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works well for either.

Curious about CBT for anxiety? Here are 5 techniques to try.

The difference between having social anxiety and being introverted comes down to preference versus fear. Introversion is a preference about how you recharge — social time drains your energy, but it doesn't fill you with dread. Social anxiety, meanwhile, brings a fear of judgment or embarrassment, often strong enough to make you skip things you'd enjoy.

It’s not unusual to have more than one anxiety disorder at the same time, and they can show up alongside other conditions including depression. A doctor can help you sort out which ones you’re dealing with, and treatments like CBT can target several disorders at once.

A specific phobia and agoraphobia differ in what the fear is tied to. A specific phobia is about one clear trigger, such as spiders or flying. Agoraphobia is broader: it's a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help, like a crowd or public transit.

The most common types of anxiety in adults are specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Altogether, anxiety disorders affect close to 1 in 5 U.S. adults each year and are the most prevalent type of mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders can ease on their own for some people, but many stick around or return without treatment. Fortunately, treatment can meaningfully improve your quality of life. Most people find that therapy, medication, or a combination makes a noticeable difference.

The most well-supported therapy for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), often paired with gradual exposure work. Medication is another option with strong evidence, either used alone or alongside therapy. The right fit depends on your specific disorder and its severity, so it's important to consult a professional.

There are several natural ways to manage anxiety, though they aren’t a replacement for clinical treatment. Regular exercise, quality sleep, and cutting back on caffeine and alcohol can all help alleviate how anxious you feel day to day. Mindfulness practices (like breathing exercises or grounding techniques) are especially well-supported, since they teach you to notice anxious thoughts or sensations without getting swept up in them.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9641. V&A proposing significant cuts to its academy amid financial pressures

The V&A has offered adult courses for decades, drawing on its collections and curators in a tradition that goes back to the museum’s origins as a school of design

The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) has drawn up plans to dismantle much of the V&A Academy, a significant part of its adult-learning programme, by the end of the year, The Art Newspaper has learned. Around 50% of the Academy’s staff may be cut and the future of flagship courses are under threat. Senior figures in other parts of the museum have also been asked to propose cuts to their teams, according to people familiar with the plans.

The V&A has offered adult courses for decades, drawing on its collections and curators in a tradition that goes back to the museum’s origins as a school of design. In 2016 it launched the Learning Academy to run much of its learning programmes. It was later renamed V&A Academy, which today runs expert-led courses, practical workshops and talks. Its courses are taught mainly at the V&A’s South Kensington site and online.

The proposals for cuts to the Academy, which sits within the museum’s commercial department, were communicated to staff on 5 October and justified by management on the grounds that the programme had failed to meet income expectations, according to people with direct knowledge of the discussions. The changes would see many of the Academy’s in-person courses at South Kensington brought to an end, including flagship courses relaunched this year in a ten-week format, with a hybrid option allowing students to attend in person or online.

The Academy’s African heritage programme and professional-development courses for museum-sector workers are among the activities expected to be retained. Selected on-demand and live online courses are also expected to continue.

The consultation period for staff to discuss the proposals with management and provide feedback is due to end today (26 October), according to people with knowledge of the matter that The Art Newspaper spoke to.

The Art Newspaper has spoken to current staff members and others with knowledge of the plans, all of whom asked not to be named for fear of repercussions. “Nobody had any inkling this was going to happen,” says one staff member. Another adds that the museum is “full of people who are feeling very demoralised”. If the proposals go ahead, the Academy will cease to operate in its current form by the end of the year, according to people with knowledge of the plans.

A V&A spokesperson said in a statement sent to The Art Newspaper: “We are currently reviewing the V&A Academy offer and the way in which this is delivered as part of wider efforts to streamline activity and identify efficiencies across our operations to ensure they are financially sustainable and deliver maximum impact. We are still in the consultation phase, and no final decisions have been made, but the current proposals will see us continue to deliver an adult learning programme." The spokesperson made clear that the V&A would not be able to comment further at this time.

The proposed restructuring is striking in light of the Academy’s recent reported performance. The V&A’s 2024–25 annual report says the Academy recorded sales of £1.2m, an increase of more than 22% on the previous year, while its contribution to the museum rose by more than 60% to £365,000.

The 2025–26 annual report does not provide a full breakdown of the Academy’s annual income, expenditure or profit. Instead, it describes the Academy’s hybrid learning strategy as “combining scalable online formats with high-impact in-person art history experiences”, saying the approach expanded the programme’s “reach and resilience” during its first full year and “consolidated” the growth achieved the previous year.

The report also records that the hybrid course Arts of Japan “contributed to V&A Academy’s biggest ever quarter in spring 2026, when total sales exceeded £400,000”.

At the time of writing, one of the Academy’s five flagship 10-week hybrid courses, A History of London: 1066–1666, was marked as sold out on the museum’s website. People familiar with the proposals say all five courses, including Arts of Japan and A History of London, are expected to be discontinued.

The proposed cuts come after a series of challenges for the V&A in recent months, including allegations of racism reported byThe Art Newspaper in July and strikes over pay and working conditions in September. The disputes over conditions continue: on 19 October, the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union and Prospect announced further strike action across all four V&A sites (South Kensington, East Museum, East Storehouse and Young V&A) on 29 and 30 October. However, statements sent to The Art Newspaper today from both unions said that their members have suspended strike action, to allow for further talks after an “improved offer” from the museum.

The V&A has also launched a voluntary exit scheme open to staff across the institution, which is expected to close on 26 October, according to people with knowledge of its terms. In response to The Art Newspaper’s October report on the voluntary exit scheme, a spokesperson said inflation, economic uncertainty and reduced visitor spending were contributing to financial pressures, while below-inflation government settlements would reduce funding in real terms over the coming years. The V&A’s 2025–26 annual report records a 30% rise in retail net sales to £15.7m.

The accounts show that the museum received £59.9m in government grant-in-aid during the year, up from £56.2m in 2024–25 and representing 42% of the group’s income. A further £5.2m was awarded through the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund to support essential work to protect the buildings at South Kensington and Young V&A.

The proposals to make cuts at the Academy come against the backdrop of a major expansion of the V&A’s estate, including the opening of V&A East Storehouse in May 2025 and V&A East Museum in April 2026. Some staff believe the South Kensington museum is bearing the cost of expenditure associated with the new east London sites. “We suspect that the South Kensington site is paying for the financial problems associated with V&A East,” says one staff member.

Prospect’s national secretary for heritage, Paula Lamont, tells The Art Newspaper in a statement: “Our members are concerned that the financial cost of opening new sites is falling on them, rather than being absorbed in other areas. Heaping more workload and pressure on an increasingly demoralised workforce is unsustainable and cannot be the answer.”

According to a report by Arts Professional, the PCS union has claimed that the institution is projecting cumulative operational deficits of £19m by 2030. The V&A did not address the figure when asked by The Art Newspaper. Its latest annual report rates the risk to longer-term financial sustainability as high. It says: “Mitigations through commercial growth and cost reduction have been identified and form a central tenet of the V&A’s new five-year strategy 2026-30.”

The terms offered to V&A Academy staff remain unclear, with concerns that those with less than two years’ service may not qualify for statutory redundancy pay under UK law. The Academy has around 17 permanent staff, but its courses also feature guest lecturers from across the museum and beyond. According to information available via the V&A’s website, for 12 of the Academy’s courses this autumn, five hybrid and seven online-only, there are around 100 lecturers and speakers besides Academy staff, from curators elsewhere in the V&A to freelance lecturers and visiting academics, suggesting the effects of any cuts could be felt far outside the Academy.

Staff are also concerned about proposed cuts to teams across the wider museum, believed to be around 10-15%, which are expected to affect curatorial roles. A former senior member of staff who witnessed the V&A’s 2021 post pandemic restructuring, when approximately 15–20% of staff were let go, says curatorial and conservation teams are not among the museum’s largest costs and are important to its ability to safeguard collections, attract donors and develop projects. Cutting expertise, they argue, risks undermining the very work that helps secure donations.

The proposals have also surprised some in light of the museum’s director, Tristram Hunt, having served in education-focused roles previously. A historian and former Labour MP, Hunt served as shadow education secretary and has a reputation for championing learning.

The V&A’s annual report describes its purpose as promoting public enjoyment and understanding of art, craft and design, including through study and research. Its founder, Henry Cole, placed education and public access at the heart of the museum’s mission, a legacy that the proposed changes risk undermining, according to people familiar with the plans.

“Henry Cole will be spinning in his grave,” says one.

#9640. How to define cheating in a relationship (and what to do about it)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Late-night texts lighting up their phone. A “friend from work” who comes up a little too often when they talk about their day. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and it’s a name you've conveniently left out of your story. Either way, it leads to a quiet, nagging sense that something's off.

Some cheating is obvious. But the old idea that it only counts if it's physical doesn't hold up to how people experience betrayal today. Emotional connections can form through a screen, and it isn't always a single, clear-cut act.

Here’s the big picture on what cheating really means, and what to do if you’re facing it in your own relationship.

Cheating means acting in a way that violates the boundaries and trust that a couple has built together.

The issue is that the boundaries aren’t always clear. Many couples never discuss what's off limits, whether that’s a text to an ex, a close emotional friendship, or a flirtatious dinner. You and your partner may share the same values, and assume you’re aligned on the specifics. Then a moment reveals you’re not.

Where people draw the line on cheating usually traces back to a few underlying factors.

Attachment style: People prone to relationship anxiety may read more behaviors as threatening. People who lean more avoidant may downplay concerning behavior as trivial, including their own.

Cultural and religious background: Some cultures and religions view certain dating norms, like close friendships outside the relationship, as completely normal, while others see them as concerning.

Relationship structure: Couples set their own rules for the relationship, whether that’s monogamy, non-monogamy, or somewhere in between. Those rules define what counts as betrayal.

Related read: How to find your attachment style and deepen your relationships

Infidelity takes many forms, and even within each form, it can look drastically different depending on the situation. Here’s how it tends to show up.

This is the one most people picture first: romantic or sexual contact with someone outside the relationship, without your partner knowing or agreeing to it. That last part is key.

Couples in open relationships can have very different lines. As long as both partners are on the same page, physical intimacy with others can be a normal part of the relationship.

Emotional cheating means forming a close bond with someone outside your relationship that pulls closeness or energy away from your partner.

The line between a close friendship and an emotional affair can feel blurry, but research points to three signs:

Details get shared that don't get shared with your partner.

An unspoken attraction exists, even if neither person names it.

Emotional cheating can be dismissed because nothing physical happened, but many people find it just as painful as physical infidelity, sometimes more so. It tends to build slowly, until the loyalty has quietly shifted.

Virtual cheating is physical or emotional cheating through a screen. This can look like sexting, intimate messaging, or building a close connection online. Some therapists also include excessive pornography use when it's hidden and gets in the way of intimacy with a partner, though opinions vary.

This type of cheating is more accessible than most other forms of infidelity, and is often harder to catch. A message is one tap away, at any hour, with virtually anyone.

Micro-cheating involves smaller, ambiguous behaviors that fall short of the categories above, but can still chip away at trust. Some common examples include:

Keeping a dating profile active "just in case"

Finding constant reasons to message one specific person

Spending time with someone without mentioning it to your partner

Flirting with someone in a way you wouldn't if your partner were present

It comes down to whether it's a repeated pattern your partner wouldn't be okay with.

Financial infidelity means hiding money, concealing debt, keeping secret accounts, or making big financial decisions without telling your partner. It's a serious trust issue, especially in long-term relationships where finances are shared.

This is more common than most people expect and can do just as much damage as other forms of infidelity.

If you’re suspicious of your partner, sitting with that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But before you act on a hunch, try slowing down and approaching the situation with as much calm as you can.

Start by noticing what’s actually happening—and what’s actually changed—versus what you suspect. Has your partner’s communication, availability, or emotional presence shifted in a specific way? Or is this more of a gut sense that something's off?

Both are valid, but knowing which one you’re dealing with can help you decide how to proceed.

💙 Explore Sensations vs. Emotions with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your unease may not be about your suspicions. It might be disconnection, feeling unappreciated, or a sense that something’s changed between you. Getting clear on what’s bugging you before you bring it up can make the conversation more productive.

💙 Dig deeper with Investigating Anxiety from the Emotions Series on Calm.

You may think that checking their phone, socials, or location data will settle your suspicion about the situation. But it tends to worsen your anxiety.

If you find something, you’re left dealing with what you found and the fact that you went looking. If you don’t, the relief rarely lasts, because whatever made you suspicious in the first place is still unresolved.

A few minutes of focused breathing before a hard conversation can settle your body and quiet your mind. That short reset can help you feel steadier and lead to a clearer conversation for both of you.

💙 Take a Pause to Breathe on the Calm app.

Before you bring something up, think about what you’re hoping for. Do you want clarity? Reassurance? That goal can keep you focused, even if the conversation gets derailed.

Approaching the discussion with an open mind, rather than jumping to accusations, often invites a more honest exchange.

Instead of starting with “I think you’re cheating on me,” try something along the lines of “I’ve been feeling disconnected and I’d like to talk about it.”

Whether you're dealing with confirmed infidelity or unresolved suspicion, you don't have to process it alone. Support from a therapist, individually or as a couple, can offer a structured space to work through it.

Sometimes suspicion itself, even without proof of cheating, may be a sign that the relationship needs attention.

Cheating is a violation of the spoken or unspoken agreements you and your partner have made about exclusivity. It can show up physically, emotionally, or virtually, and what counts can look different from couple to couple. Secrecy and broken trust are usually the common thread.

Read more: Here's how to work through the most common relationship issues

The main types of cheating are physical, emotional, and virtual, though subtler patterns such as financial secrecy or "micro-cheating" can apply too.

Physical cheating involves intimate contact outside the relationship. Emotional cheating involves a close bond kept hidden from your partner. Virtual cheating involves a romantic connection through a screen.

Emotional cheating can feel just as harmful as physical cheating, and for some people, more so. It often builds slowly, through shared thoughts and private moments your partner doesn't know about.

Physical cheating usually involves specific, identifiable moments, while emotional cheating often unfolds gradually, as loyalty fades over time.

Cheating almost always involves some kind of concealment. Being vague, withholding details, or keeping a connection secret are all forms of it. Sometimes it's the hiding, more than the act itself, that turns it into a betrayal.

Couples can define cheating differently, based on their values, culture, and the specific agreements they've made. Partners in open relationships, for example, may knowingly allow behaviors that other couples wouldn't. What’s important is that you and your partner are on the same page about boundaries.

Disagreements over what’s considered cheating are worth addressing head-on. A transparent conversation about your expectations and boundaries can feel uncomfortable, but it's one of the more protective things you can do for a relationship. A couples therapist can support this conversation if it feels overwhelming to navigate alone.

When you’re talking to your partner about what’s bothering you, try focusing on your own experience rather than their behavior. Something like "I've been feeling distant and want to check in with us" opens the door for an honest conversation instead of a defensive one.

In some cases, trust can be rebuilt after cheating, though it takes consistent effort from both of you. Many couples find professional support helpful along the way.

It usually requires transparency and accountability to understand what led to the breach. Leaving is a valid choice too, as long as the decision is made carefully.

Read more: Recovering from infidelity: 6 tips to help couples heal from an affair

#9639. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

#9637. Fake or Fortune art historian donates major Anglo-Indian art collection to Tate

Rudolph Swoboda, A Sepoy in HH Maharaja Srinagar’s Indian Regiment, 23 Years Old (around 1886)

A UK collector has donated a significant collection of 50 works by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries to the Tate in London. The collection, given by the UK art historian Charles Greig, includes works by Indian artists, such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan, and European artists, including Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, along with British figures such as Thomas Daniell and William Daniell.

The works throw light on a “period of profound cultural, social and political change brought about by British colonialism in South Asia” says a Tate statement. Key pieces donated include three watercolours by Sita Ram who was instrumental in creating works known as “Company paintings”, watercolours created in a European style for foreign patrons. The British Library in London has a large collection of watercolours by Ram.

Sita Ram, The Palace at Murshidabad from the River (around 1814-15) Presented by Charles Andrew Greig

Greig says in a statement: “Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770. Assembling this collection has been my life’s primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”

Asked why Greig opted for Tate, a spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper: “Tate has long held a few key paintings related to Anglo-Indian history of the period, including Zoffany’s Colonel Mordant’s Cock Match (around 1784) and Indian landscapes by Thomas Daniell and William Hodges”. Greig recently appeared in an episode of the television series Fake or Fortune?, in which he assessed a portrait of an Indian woman by the 18th-century Scottish artist Katherine Read.

A free display of the works drawn from the Greig collection is due to open at Tate Britain in 2028.

The works—mostly by Greek artists—will go to the National Gallery of Greece in Athens, Momus-Museum of Contemporary Art Thessaloniki, the Museum of Contemporary Art of Crete and National Galleries Scotland in Edinburgh

#9635. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

#9634. How to dream more: 6 tips to increase how often you dream

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We all know that one person who says, “You’ll never believe what I dreamt last night!” Many people who dream can become obsessed with the stories their minds show them at night. Some people believe their dreams provide insights into their subconscious, while others say they inspire creativity. And those who aren’t into the deep dream interpretation simply like the fantasy world that their minds create when they’re asleep.

If you’re fascinated by your dreams for any of these reasons, you might want to learn how to dream more and make your dreams more vivid. And while you can’t control everything—like the inevitable falling nightmare everyone has had at least once—you can do things to dream more frequently and to make those dreams easier to recall. Here are a few simple techniques and lifestyle changes you might want to try to make the most of the time you spend asleep.

When you sleep better, you’re more likely to enter the rapid eye movement (REM) part of your sleep cycle, when most dreaming occurs. This sleep cycle may increase the chances of having more frequent and vivid dreams, so here are a few tips to encourage deeper sleep.

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help regulate your sleep cycle and increase the likelihood of dreaming. To get enough REM sleep, aim for 7–9 hours of sleep each night.

💙 Try relaxing an hour before bed with Soften Into Sleep, a meditation that can help you release tension at night.

Read, take a warm bath, or practice mindfulness to ease into rest and create an environment for dreaming. Avoid screens for at least an hour before bed, as the blue light can disrupt your body’s natural sleep-wake cycle. If you must use devices, try a blue light filter or dim your screen.

💙 Explore these nine tips to help you build a better bedtime routine.

To improve sleep quality and increase your chances of dreaming, keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. The ideal temperature is about 60–67 degrees Fahrenheit (or 15–19 degrees Celsius). Use blackout curtains to block light, earplugs or a white noise machine to drown out noise, and invest in a comfortable mattress and pillows to support your posture.

Lastly, keep your bedroom tidy and use it only for sleep and relaxation if you can. This can help you create a mental association between your bedroom and restful sleep.

💙 Press play on one of our relaxing Soundscapes, like White Noise Ocean Surf, to help you drift off to sleep.

Practice meditation, yoga, or deep breathing exercises to help decrease anxiety so you can get a good night’s sleep, which may promote more vivid dreaming. Regular exercise can help too, but remember to avoid vigorous activity too close to bedtime.

💙 Keep stress at bay by tuning into 7 Days of Managing Stress, a stress reduction series hosted by Tamara Levitt.

Heavy meals, caffeine, or alcohol before bed can disrupt sleep and decrease dream frequency. Opt for light snacks if you're hungry, and avoid caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime.

💙 Add mindfulness to mealtime with our session on the Benefits of Mindful Eating.

Drink water throughout the day to support sleep quality, but try to limit water intake about an hour before bed to prevent trips to the bathroom in the middle of the night.

During your wind down routine, you can sip teas like chamomile or valerian root. These are thought to have calming effects that may promote relaxation and improve sleep quality, which may lead to more vivid dreams.

💙 Listen to a relaxing Sleep Story before bed, like Why Do We Sleep, while sipping tea as part of a new nighttime ritual.

Sleep is divided into several stages that cycle throughout the night, typically lasting about 90 minutes per cycle.

Stage 1 (light sleep): This is a transitional phase where you drift in and out of sleep.

Stage 2 (deeper light sleep): Your body temperature drops and your heart rate begins to slow.

Stage 3 (deep sleep): Known as slow-wave sleep, this stage promotes physical recovery and health.

REM sleep: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, where your brain activity increases and your eyes move rapidly under your eyelids, is when the most vivid dreams occur.

Melatonin is a hormone your body naturally produces that helps to regulate your sleep-wake cycles. Levels rise in the evening to help you feel sleepy and decrease in the morning to help you wake up. Some people take melatonin supplements to help with sleep issues like insomnia, jet lag, or other sleep disorders, but it may also affect your dreams.

Some studies suggest that melatonin may enhance REM sleep. This might lead to more frequent and vivid dreams, and some people who take melatonin report more intense and memorable dreams.

Melatonin may also help with dream recall by enhancing overall sleep quality.

The effect of melatonin on dreams can vary from person to person. Remember to always consult a medical professional before you take any supplement, as they can interact with other medications or simply not be right for you.

People like remembering their dreams for a number of reasons. Perhaps it sparks their curiosity about what they could be feeling on a subconscious level or could provide them with an escape from reality. Whatever your reason for wanting to remember your dreams may be, dream recall can become easier and more natural with time and practice.

Keep a dream journal: Write down your dreams as soon as you wake up, even if you can only remember bits and pieces of them. Over time, this can train your brain to pay more attention to your dreams. Review your dream journal during the day to help reinforce your memory and increase your chances of remembering future dreams.

Set an intention: Before you go to sleep, reinforce your desire to remember your dreams. Repeating a phrase like "I will remember my dreams" may increase your chances of recalling them when you wake up.

Stay still upon waking: Moving too quickly when you wake up can cause you to forget your dreams, so before you get out of bed, lie still for a few moments and try to focus on your dream. Sometimes a single image or emotion can trigger the memory of the entire dream.

Reflect on your day: Before bed, think about your day and journal about it. This can help create a connection between your waking and dreaming life and associate both with memories and self-reflection. Thus, this practice may make it easier to remember your dreams.

Practice mindfulness: Regular mindfulness and meditation practice can improve your overall awareness and attention, including your ability to remember dreams. Meditate before bed to clear your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. These six tips for meditating in bed can help you get started.

Wake up naturally: Waking up suddenly can startle you into thinking intensely about the here and now, making it harder to remember dreams, so try to avoid using an alarm clock if you can. Pay attention to your body's natural sleep cycles and try to go to bed early enough to wake up naturally. If you need an alarm, set one that wakes you gently, perhaps with soft sounds or a sunrise effect.

Vivid dreams can be more engaging and memorable than other forms of dreaming that are less detailed.

Before falling asleep, visualize a recent dream or imagine a scenario you’d like to dream about in as much detail as possible. This can help stimulate your mind and lead to more vivid dreams.

Experiment with different sleeping positions to see if they influence the vividness of your dreams.

Get natural light during the day and reduce light exposure before bed to help regulate your sleep cycle and improve the quality of your REM sleep. Improving your sleep cycles and natural circadian rhythm may lead to more vivid dreams.

Creative activities like drawing, writing, or playing music can stimulate your imagination and enhance your dreams.

Meditate before bed to help calm your mind and prepare for a restful night’s sleep. This may increase the chances of having vivid dreams. As you’re releasing stresses from the day, you may create space for your subconscious mind to flourish as you rest. These 10 mindful activities can help you release stress quickly at the end of the day.

Some people use supplements like galantamine, choline, or vitamin B6 to try to enhance dream vividness. Consult a healthcare provider before using any supplements, as they can have side effects and interactions with other medications you’re already taking.

Once you’re remembering your dreams most mornings, you might get curious about steering them. That’s lucid dreaming: knowing you’re dreaming while it’s happening, which can let you look around, change the scene, or just enjoy the ride.

It takes practice, and it doesn’t happen for everyone. The good news is that things you may already be doing, like keeping a dream journal and setting an intention before bed, are also how many people start learning it.

If you’re curious, our step-by-step guide can help you learn how to lucid dream, with techniques like reality checks, MILD, and wake back to bed.

Certain foods and nutrients may influence your dreaming patterns. For example, foods containing tryptophan, like turkey and dairy products, can promote sleepiness and may impact the quality of your dreams. Foods rich in vitamin B6, like bananas, chickpeas, fish, and fortified cereals, may help with recall.

Eat a balanced diet with a variety of nutrients to support your overall sleep health, and avoid heavy meals and caffeine close to bedtime, as they can disrupt sleep and reduce dream frequency.

Several factors can affect your ability to remember dreams.

Poor sleep quality, such as disruptions in your sleep cycle, can hinder dream recall.

Stress or anxiety can interfere with sleep and make it harder to remember your dreams.

Sleep disorders like insomnia, sleep apnea, and restless leg syndrome disrupt sleep and impact dream recall.

Some medications, particularly those that affect the central nervous system, can interfere with dreaming.

Alcohol and drugs can alter sleep patterns and reduce the likelihood of remembering dreams.

A lack of interest in dreams can mean the brain doesn’t focus on retaining them.

Sleep disorders can significantly impact dreaming. Insomnia, which makes it difficult to fall or stay asleep, can reduce the amount of REM sleep you get, leading to fewer dreams and poorer dream recall.

Sleep apnea causes repeated interruptions in breathing during sleep, disrupting REM sleep cycles and reducing the frequency and vividness of dreams. Treatments like CPAP therapy for sleep apnea may improve sleep quality and dreaming.

Restless leg syndrome can also interfere with falling and staying asleep, which can impact dream frequency and recall.

Narcolepsy is marked by excessive daytime sleepiness and fragmented nighttime sleep. It may lead to vivid (and sometimes bizarre) dreams or dream-like hallucinations.

Generally, there are few risks to trying to dream more. Supplements like melatonin or galantamine may cause side effects or interact with other medications, so talk to your doctor before taking them.

Paying more attention to your dreams can sometimes lead to more vivid nightmares, especially if you have underlying anxiety or stress.

Understanding your dreams may reveal hidden thoughts, fears, and desires, and can help process emotions, particularly those you may not fully address during waking life. This may help in emotional healing.

Dreams can also offer creative solutions to problems or provide new perspectives for challenges you face in waking life.

#9633. Art Basel Qatar releases 2027 exhibitor list as renewed threat of war looms over Gulf

Art Basel Qatar 2027 will return to the M7 and Doha Design District from 28-30 January

Art Basel Qatar (ABQ), the Qatari state's finely orchestrated selling event in partnership with the Swiss fair giant, today announced the exhibitor list for its second edition, which will take place across the M7 and Doha Design District venues from 28 to 30 January 2027 (VIP preview days 26-27 January).

Eighty-two galleries plan to take part, a slight decrease from the 87 that showed in the inaugural edition. Among them are Sylvia Kouvali (London, Piraeus) bringing the kinetic art pioneer Liliane Lijn, and Gagosian, which will offer works by the art-world prankster Maurizio Catellan. Like the inaugural edition, almost half of participating galleries operate spaces in the Menasa (Middle East, North Africa and South Asia) region, including Marfa’ Projects from Beirut, whose stand will feature the Lebanese artist Stéphanie Saadé, and India’s Nature Morte, presenting the architecturally minded sculptor Ayesha Singh.

Each presentation will respond to the theme of “between”, which was chosen by the fair’s artistic director, the Iraqi curator Wassan Al-Khudhairi, who was the founding director of Doha’s Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art from 2007-12. She takes the reins from Wael Shawky, who curated the inaugural edition.

Exhibitor turnover is high from last year’s edition, with 35 galleries—or around 40%—not returning, including global dealerships like Hauser & Wirth, Pace, Almine Rech and Victoria Miro, as well as prominent regional spaces such as Gallery Isabelle from Dubai. Filling their places are 30 newcomers: Isla Flotante (Buenos Aires, São Paulo), Pilar Corrias (London) and Silverlens (Manila, New York) are among those taking part for the first time.

A full list of galleries exhibiting at Art Basel Qatar 2027—plus those not returning—can be found at the end of this article.

Vincenzo De Bellis, Art Basel’s global director of fairs, tells The Art Newspaper the high turnover is typical of ABQ’s format. “Across our global fairs, we see greater turnover in the sectors that are theme-led, and in Qatar that approach extends to the fair as a whole. Selection is closely tied to how galleries’ proposed solo presentations respond to each edition’s theme, so it is natural for the exhibitor list to change from year to year.”

Gallerists in the selection committee are: Lorenzo Fischi, Galleria Continua; Gordon VeneKlasen, VeneKlasen Gallery; Daniela Gareh, White Cube; Shireen Gandhy, Chemould Prescott Road; Sunny Rahbar, The Third Line; and Mohammed Hafiz, Athr.

Like its competitors, Art Basel does not discuss motivations behind individual exhibitor applications, including whether some prospective applicants may have pulled out due to geopolitical tensions in the Arabian Gulf. Nonetheless, visitors planning their trip to Qatar next year will certainly be conscious of renewed bombardment in neighbouring Saudi Arabia earlier this month, and looming threats of the US and Israel resuming war with Iran. In late February, a few weeks after the conclusion of the first Art Basel Qatar, Iran launched missiles into Qatar, injuring 16 people, according to Qatari authorities at the time, and causing major disruptions to its airspace.

As a contingency plan, should the fair be postponed or considerably altered due to such circumstances, exhibitors will receive a refund of their participation fee or have the option to defer their participation to the following edition, currently planned for January 2028. Nonetheless, any last-minute drop outs will be subject to a standard penalty fee, similar to other Art Basel fairs.

While this uncertainty might deter some galleries, others will likely be incentivised by the unusually generous level of support provided to exhibitors via Art Basel's partnership with Qatar Sports Investments (QSI) and QC+, the commercial branch of Qatar Museums. This funds customs clearance, in-country transportation, consolidated storage and installation services, hotel accommodation for up to two staff members, and travel and hotel costs for exhibiting artists. In addition, from the 2027 edition Art Basel Qatar will also cover 50% of outbound shipping costs for unsold works, up to a maximum of $20,000 per gallery, further mitigating costs and risks for galleries.

Art Basel is also deepening its roots in Qatar by launching a year-round programme there to develop the country’s art market, including masterclasses and workshops designed to foster new collectors. "Our ambition extends well beyond the fair week: through our new year-round programme, we aim to deepen collector engagement between editions and contribute to the sustained growth of the regional art market," Art Basel's chief executive Noah Horowitz says in a statement.

Visitors to the second edition of ABQ will also get a chance to see the inaugural Rubaiya, a quadrennial exhibition in Doha, that will bring together more than 120 artists, including Saodat Ismailova and Rirkrit Tiravanija.
